metadata.title: Small Language Models.
metadata.note: Standalone teaching explainer (~2.5min) on Small Language Models (SLMs). FRAMEWORK-FIRST (built to pass PROOF): definition (B01) + the reframe 'size is a trade, not a score' (B02) shown before the worked example (B03: routing support tickets); then the when-to-use rubric + falsifiability (B04: smaller isn't always better); scaffolded task (B06). ONE insight: for a narrow, repeated task a small specialized model can match a big general one while being faster, cheaper, and private — but the big model still wins for open-ended/broad/novel work. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW: no specific parameter counts, benchmarks, or model names; all comparisons qualitative. Bookends render (composer/verdict/handoff/outro via Claude Remotion comps); body B01-B04 are house-style 4K PIL cards generated by make_cards.py.

beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. When people need AI, they reach for the biggest model they can find. But small language models, SLMs, are quietly winning a lot of real jobs. So let's figure out the actual question: when is smaller the smarter choice?

narrow job → small model can match
match the model to the task

beats.narration_text: First, what an SLM even is. It's a language model, same basic idea as the big ones, but far smaller, few enough parameters to run fast, cheaply, and often right on your own hardware. And because it's small, you can fine-tune it for one specific job without a data center. Small, fast, private, and focused.

beats.narration_text: Here's the reframe. We treat model size like a quality score, bigger equals better. But size is really a trade. A big general model carries huge knowledge and strong reasoning, and it's slow, expensive, and lives in the cloud. A small specialized model knows less, but for a narrow task it can match the giant, while being faster, cheaper, and private.

beats.narration_text: Take one real job: routing support tickets to the right team. You don't need a model that can also write poetry and debug code. Fine-tune a small model on your own tickets, and it routes them as well as a frontier model, at a fraction of the cost and latency, and it never leaves your servers. Narrow job, small model, better fit.

beats.narration_text: But smaller is not always better, that's the trap in reverse. For open-ended reasoning, broad world knowledge, or a novel one-off problem, the big model still wins, that's what the extra size buys. So the rule: reach for a small model when the task is narrow, repeated, and sensitive to cost, speed, or privacy. Reach for a big one when it's open-ended, or you only need it once.

beats.narration_text: So stop defaulting to the biggest model. Size is a trade, not a score. For a narrow, repeated job, a small specialized model is often faster, cheaper, private, and just as good. Match the model to the task.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick one AI task you run over and over, classifying, tagging, routing, extracting. Ask: does this really need a frontier model, or just a small one fine-tuned on my data? Estimate what you'd save on cost and latency. That's usually where a small model earns its place.
